items.title: OneLake table APIs: Now with Iceberg writes, plus richer table metadata (Preview)
items.excerpt: OneLake table APIs already let Iceberg-compatible engines discover and read tables in Microsoft Fabric. Today we're taking the next step with two additions: Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) writes through the OneLake table endpoint, now available, and a new additional table metadata API, in preview, for adding descriptions and tags to tables and columns. Together, they make OneLake a place where any engine can not only read data, but also publish it, with the business context people and AI agents need to use it well. Write native Iceberg tables from the engines you already use Until now, the OneLake Iceberg endpoint supported read-only metadata operations. Now, IRC-compatible clients can create native Iceberg tables, commit new snapshots, and request short-lived storage credentials through the same endpoint they already use for reads. That means engines such as PyIceberg, Snowflake, and DuckDB can land results directly in OneLake using standard Iceberg tooling, with no custom connectors or copy jobs. items.title: Bring your Fabric data into your next app with connectors
items.excerpt: Most business applications start with data that already exists. Customer orders may live in a Fabric SQL database. Inventory history may be in a Lakehouse. Sales performance may already be modeled in Power BI. The opportunity is not to move that data again, but to turn trusted data into an experience that helps people make decisions and take action. Connectors in Fabric Apps shorten that path. They give an app a consistent way to work with Fabric data, so developers can spend less time on integration plumbing and more time building the experience users need. Connect to the Fabric data you already trust. Build the experience your users need. Keep the application close to the data and governance foundation already in place. Instead of beginning with infrastructure, start with the customer's need: What should this app help someone understand, decide, or do? items.title: Govern Fabric connections with admin APIs and data connection policies (Preview)
items.excerpt: Co-author: Abhishek Narain Protect continuity, understand connection risk, and set tenant-wide guardrails Imagine that the person who built a business-critical pipeline has left your organization. The connection still exists, but nobody is sure who can manage it or whether its credentials will keep working. What begins as a handover problem quickly becomes a governance question: who owns your connections, where do they lead, and which identities should be allowed to use them? Microsoft Fabric brings these questions together through two complementary capabilities: Admin connection APIs give tenant administrators visibility and ownership-management tools across connection types. Data connection policies set preventive controls for cloud connections. Together, they support a practical sequence: restore responsibility, understand your connections, then enforce the authentication boundaries your organization needs. From recovery to prevention Keep work moving when a connection owner leaves A departure should not leave a connection without someone who can maintain it. items.title: Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake (Preview)
items.excerpt: A customer reports a missing delivery. The service case is in Salesforce, while the shipping and returns records are in Microsoft Fabric. Before a team can decide what to do next, it needs to connect those two views of the same customer experience. For many organizations, answering questions like this still means exporting customer data, building ingestion pipelines, and maintaining another copy for analytics. Every additional handoff adds work for data teams and another dataset to secure and reconcile. Business teams wait for a complete picture while customer decisions move ahead. Zero-copy file sharing offers a different approach by making source data available where it is needed for analysis, without first building a separate ingestion copy. The data is always current. This makes it easier to connect customer context with the financial, operational, and product information that gives it meaning. Introducing Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake Salesforce Data 360 Integration with OneLake is now available in preview. items.title: Find expensive queries from Capacity Metrics (Generally Available)
items.excerpt: When warehouse capacity usage spikes, you need to quickly understand what ran, which warehouse drove the usage, and which queries require investigation. The Monitor in warehouse action in the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app connects the capacity-level view directly to Warehouse Monitor. It opens the selected warehouse with the relevant time window already applied, eliminating manual correlation across monitoring experiences. Figure: Animated GIF - demonstrating how to navigate from a Capacity Metrics timepoint to Warehouse Monitor in four steps. Follow the activity into your warehouse Open Capacity Metrics: From the Compute page, select your capacity and review CU % over time. Capacity Units, or CUs, represent the compute consumption tracked for the capacity. Choose a timepoint : Select the usage increase you want to investigate, and then select Explore and open TimePoint Detail. Choose an operation window: Under Background operations for time range, select a supported warehouse query operation whose Start and End times cover the interval. Then select Monitor in warehouse. Explore Warehouse Monitor: Open Query history to review statements that ran during the selected interval

As adoption grows, that freedom becomes even more valuable. So does the ability to protect the settings that matter most. A workspace admin role brings broad responsibility. But owning an analytics workspace shouldn't mean every administrator also needs authority over its encryption and networking. Organizations need a more precise way to share responsibility, without pulling everyday workspace management back into a central team's queue. At FabCon Barcelona, we introduced the Allow workspace settings editing policy, part of Microsoft Fabric policies, currently in preview. We're excited to give organizations finer control over sensitive workspace changes while keeping teams in charge of their day-to-day work. Now, you can delegate workspace ownership with clearer boundaries around who can change what, and where. items.title: Access versioned lakeFS data from Microsoft Fabric with Microsoft OneLake shortcuts
items.excerpt: Coauthor: Iddo Avneri (Treeverse) Use a live branch for up-to-date analytics or pin a shortcut to an immutable commit when reproducibility matters. Data teams often need two seemingly conflicting things: immediate access to the latest data and the ability to return to the exact data behind an earlier analysis, report, or experiment. Maintaining both typically means creating snapshots, copying datasets, or building additional pipelines. That adds operational overhead and makes it harder to know which version of the data was used. Microsoft OneLake and lakeFS provide a simpler, complementary pattern for addressing this use case. OneLake shortcuts allow Microsoft Fabric lakehouses to reference data in external storage through a unified namespace. Because lakeFS exposes versioned data through an S3-compatible gateway , Fabric can access lakeFS-managed datasets by using a OneLake S3-compatible shortcut. The result: Fabric users can access either the current data on a lakeFS branch or an immutable version from a specific commit.
